Poverty means the state of being very poor — a condition in which a person or group of people lacks enough money, resources, or basic necessities to live a decent life.

When we say someone lives "in poverty," we mean they struggle to afford things that most people consider essential: food, clean water, a safe place to sleep, clothing, healthcare, and education.
What "Basic Necessities" Actually Means

This is important to understand. Poverty isn't just about having less money than others. It's about not having enough to survive or live with dignity. The bare minimum a human being needs includes:

  • Food – enough to eat and stay healthy
  • Shelter – a safe, stable place to live
  • Clothing – clothes suitable for the weather and conditions
  • Healthcare – access to medical help when sick
  • Clean water and sanitation – safe water to drink and basic hygiene

When a person cannot reliably access these things, they are considered to be living in poverty.
Two Main Types of Poverty

Understanding these two types will sharpen your grasp of the word significantly.

1. Absolute Poverty
This is the most severe and straightforward form. It means a person does not have enough to survive. They may go hungry, have no shelter, or have no access to clean water or medicine. Absolute poverty is measured by a global standard — for example, the World Bank has historically defined it as surviving on less than a certain amount of money per day (like $2.15 per day as of recent years). Whether you live in India, Brazil, or anywhere else, if you fall below this line, you are in absolute poverty.

2. Relative Poverty
This is about comparison within a society. A person is in relative poverty if their income or resources are significantly below the average standard of living in their own country or community — even if they can technically survive. For example, someone in a wealthy country may have food and shelter but still be considered relatively poor because they cannot afford things that most people around them take for granted: a warm coat, school supplies for their children, a working phone, or transport to get to a job. Relative poverty is about being left behind by the society around you.
Poverty as a System, Not Just a Personal Situation

This is a crucial nuance. Poverty is not simply a personal failing or bad luck. It is often the result of large, systemic forces:

  • Lack of jobs or low wages
  • Unequal distribution of wealth in a society
  • Discrimination (based on caste, race, gender, disability, etc.)
  • Conflict, natural disasters, or political instability
  • Poor access to education or healthcare, which traps people in a cycle

Because of these forces, poverty tends to pass from one generation to the next — children born into poor families often struggle to escape poverty because they start life with fewer opportunities. This is called the poverty cycle or poverty trap.
Measuring Poverty: The Poverty Line

Governments and international organizations draw an imaginary line — called the poverty line (or poverty threshold) — to define who counts as poor. Anyone whose income falls below this line is officially considered to be living in poverty. This line is different in different countries because the cost of living varies. India, for instance, has its own poverty line based on what it costs to meet minimum needs within India.
Poverty Beyond Money: The Wider Sense

Poverty isn't always just about finances. Over time, experts have recognized that true poverty is multidimensional — meaning it has several layers:

  • Income poverty – not enough money
  • Education poverty – no access to schooling
  • Health poverty – no access to medical care
  • Digital poverty – no access to the internet or technology
  • Time poverty – so burdened with survival tasks (fetching water, working multiple jobs) that a person has no time to rest, learn, or improve their situation

When all these deprivations pile up together, they make poverty much harder to escape.
The Figurative (Non-literal) Use

In English, "poverty" is also used figuratively to describe a serious lack or deficiency of something that isn't money. This is a perfectly standard and common usage.

Examples:

  • "The speech was criticized for its poverty of ideas." → The speech had very few good or original ideas.
  • "There is a poverty of imagination in the government's plan." → The plan shows a serious lack of creativity.
  • "His writing is marked by a poverty of emotion." → His writing feels cold and emotionally thin.

In this figurative sense, "poverty of _" means a striking absence or shortage of something valuable.
Words That Live Close to "Poverty"

These are related words you'll often see used alongside or instead of poverty:

  • Destitution – an even more extreme form of poverty; total absence of resources. Destitute people have almost nothing at all.
  • Deprivation – the state of lacking things necessary for well-being; often used when talking about what someone is being denied (food deprivation, sleep deprivation).
  • Hardship – difficulty and suffering caused by lack of money or resources; slightly softer than poverty.
  • Penury – a formal/literary word for extreme poverty.
  • Indigence – another formal word meaning poverty, often used in legal or academic writing.
  • Want – in older or literary English, "want" means lack or need. "A life of want" means a life of poverty.
  • Squalor – dirty, wretched living conditions that often result from poverty.
How "Poverty" Is Used in Real Sentences

Seeing a word in action cements your understanding:

  • "About 700 million people around the world still live in extreme poverty."
  • "She grew up in poverty but worked her way through school."
  • "The government launched a new scheme to reduce rural poverty."
  • "Poverty and crime are often linked in societies with high inequality."
  • "The poverty of sanitation in the slums led to repeated disease outbreaks."
  • "His diary revealed a remarkable poverty of self-awareness." (figurative)

The Emotional and Social Weight of the Word

Finally, it's worth knowing that "poverty" is not a neutral or casual word. It carries weight. It signals suffering, injustice, and urgency. When used about real people or communities, it demands empathy and seriousness. It is not an insult — it is a description of a condition, often one that people did not choose and cannot easily escape without support.
Summary in One Paragraph

Poverty is the noun for the state of being very poor — of lacking the money, resources, or basic necessities needed to live with dignity and security. It can be absolute (not having enough to survive) or relative (having significantly less than others in the same society). It is caused not just by individual circumstances but by large social, economic, and political forces. It is multidimensional, affecting not just income but also access to education, healthcare, and opportunity. Figuratively, "poverty of" something means a serious lack of that thing. It is one of the most important and serious words in the social, economic, and humanitarian vocabulary.
